notes.meaning: Job's three companions stop answering him because he refuses to give up his claim of being blameless. They realize that nothing they say will change his mind, so they drop the debate entirely. Even though they are quiet, they still think Job is guilty and stubbornly self-righteous.

A younger man named Elihu enters the scene, burning with anger. His family comes from Buz, which traces back to Abraham's brother Nahor. He is deeply troubled because Job seemed more interested in proving himself innocent than in defending the goodness and justice of God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many historical-critical scholars view Elihu's speeches as an addition inserted into the book by a later editor rather than part of the original dialogue.

notes.meaning: Elihu is equally angry with the three older friends. They had condemned Job as a wicked hypocrite without ever proving a single charge against him. Judging a suffering person harshly without real proof is unfair and wrong.

Elihu held his tongue during the earlier speeches because Job and the three friends were older than he was. In ancient culture, younger men showed deep respect by staying silent until the elders finished speaking. Elihu waited patiently for the entire debate to come to an end.

When Elihu saw that the three older men had completely run out of arguments, his anger flared up again. He could not stay quiet while they sat helpless and defeated. He stepped forward because he believed someone needed to defend the truth.

Elihu begins his speech by acknowledging how young he is compared to the grey-haired men before him. Out of modesty and fear of being disrespectful, he held back his thoughts for a long time. It is wise and proper for younger people to listen carefully before offering their own opinions.

Elihu explains what he had expected from the debate. He thought that living many years gave people deep wisdom and understanding that they could pass on. Older people have more life experience, so it is natural to look to them for guidance first.

True wisdom does not come merely from living a long time, but from God. The Almighty breathes understanding into the human spirit that He created. Because God gives wisdom freely, even a younger person can understand what is right when taught by Him.

Elihu reminds his listeners that age and high status do not guarantee good sense. Even elderly leaders and respected teachers can fail to grasp justice and truth. Genuine insight depends on God rather than grey hair or an important title.

Since the older men have failed to solve the problem, Elihu asks them to pay attention to him. He is ready to share his own understanding of the matter. He speaks up not out of empty pride, but from a desire to speak the truth when others could not.

Elihu reminds them that he gave them his full and patient attention while they spoke. He listened closely to their lines of reasoning while they searched for words to refute Job. He earned his right to speak by first being a careful, thorough listener.

Elihu paid close attention, yet none of the three men actually refuted Job's arguments. They spoke plenty of words, but they never proved that Job was secretly guilty of the evil deeds they suspected. Accusing someone without proof does not convince anyone of the truth.

Elihu warns the three friends not to boast that they had found wisdom by leaving Job's defeat to God. They could not excuse their failed arguments by claiming that only God could bring Job down. True wisdom tackles difficult questions honestly rather than hiding behind easy excuses.

Job had not directed his complaints at Elihu, so Elihu could approach the debate without personal bitterness. Furthermore, Elihu promises not to repeat the harsh, insulting arguments the three friends had used. A fair discussion requires a calm mind and fresh reasoning.

Elihu looks at the three friends and points out that they are stunned into silence. Their flow of words has dried up, and they have nothing left to say in response to Job. Their defeat is obvious to everyone standing around.

Elihu asks whether he should keep waiting when the others are standing completely silent. Since the debate has ground to a halt, there is no reason for him to remain quiet. When those who ought to speak say nothing, others must step forward.

Elihu decides it is now his turn to take part in the discussion. He will openly declare what he knows and offer his own judgment on Job's situation. He wants to help resolve the dispute that the older men could not settle.

Elihu feels an overwhelming need to speak because his mind is crowded with thoughts and arguments. His inner spirit presses him so strongly that he can no longer hold his peace. When God's truth stirs within someone, keeping silent becomes nearly impossible.

Elihu compares his feelings to fermenting wine trapped inside sealed skins with no vent. In Bible times, fermenting juice created strong pressure that could tear a leather wineskin open if it had nowhere to escape. His thoughts are building up so much pressure that he feels ready to burst.

Elihu declares that he must speak out in order to get relief from his inner pressure. Opening his mouth to answer Job will feel like letting trapped air escape so he can breathe freely. Sharing what we know to be true brings peace to a troubled mind.

Elihu promises to be completely fair and show no favoritism toward anyone present. He will not flatter Job out of pity, nor will he flatter the older men because of their wealth or reputation. Godly counsel must always be honest rather than seeking to please people.

Elihu warns that using false flattery would invite God's immediate judgment upon him. He knows that his Creator hates dishonest praise and could take his life away in an instant. A healthy fear of God keeps a person truthful and bold when talking to others.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Older Catholic translations understand Elihu to mean that he does not know how long he has to live, so he must speak the truth without delay before death takes him.
